headline: Kawairashii is 可愛い (kawaii) plus the ending らしい (-rashii).

sources.quote: From 可愛(かわい)い (kawaii) + らしい (-rashii).

headline: Koyubi is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 指 (yubi, “finger or toe; digit”).

sources.quote: 小(こ) (ko-, “little”) + 指(ゆび) (yubi, “finger or toe; digit”)

headline: Dotchi is 何方 (dochi, “where, which way”) with a sokuon added.

sources.quote: From 何(ど)方(ち) (dochi, “where, which way”), with addition of 促(そく)音(おん) (sokuon).

headline: Kyū went from kipu through kiɸu, kiwu and kiu on its way to kyū, from Middle Chinese 級.

sources.quote: /kipu/ → /kiɸu/ → */kiwu/ → /kiu/ → /kyuː/.
From Middle Chinese 級 (MC kip).

meaning: to help (v.t.), to save, to rescue
headline: Tasukeru traces to older 助く (tasuku), a compound of 手 (ta-, “hand”) and 助く (suku, “to help”), first appearing in the late 900s.

sources.quote: From older 助(たす)く (tasuku), a compound of 手(た) (ta-, “hand”) + 助(す)く (suku, “to help”). First appears in the late 900s.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 助く entry.

headline: Eigakan is 映画 (eiga, “movie”) plus 館 (-kan, “building”).

sources.quote: From 映画(えいが) (eiga, “movie”) + 館(かん) (-kan, “building”).

headline: Kusari, “chain”, is a noun from the stem of the verb 鏈る (kusaru, “to be linked together”).

sources.quote: Noun derived from the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem form”) of verb 鏈る (kusaru, “to be linked together, to link together”).

headline: Nandemo is, by surface analysis, 何で (“why, how”) plus も.

sources.quote: By surface analysis, 何で (“why, how”) + も.

meaning: to get down, to go; come down
headline: Oriru comes from a classical upper bigrade verb, 下る (oru).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb (ラ行上二段活用) 下(お)る (oru).

headline: Taezu is the negative continuative of 絶える (taeru, “to cease”).

sources.quote: From the negative continuative form of the verb 絶える (taeru, “to cease”).

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Kawari, “substitute”, is the continuative stem of the verb 代わる (kawaru, “to substitute”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 代(か)わる (kawaru, “to substitute”).

headline: Ito, “thread”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ito.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ito.

headline: Tenisu kōto is simply English “tennis court”.

sources.quote: From English tennis court.

headline: Mono, “person”, is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 and is cognate with 物 (mono, “thing”).

sources.quote: ⟨mo₂no₂⟩ → /mono/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720. Theorized to derive from Proto-Japonic *mənə.
Cognate with 物(もの) (mono, “thing”, physical as opposed to abstract).

In ancient texts marked with pronunciation information, this character was always read as hito until around the late 800s, at which point the mono reading becomes prevalent. The mono reading has historically often been used with mild pejorative overtones, as compared to the more neutral term 人(ひと) (hito). This may suggest a broadening of the original “thing” sense for mono, which then was applied as a pejorative for a “person”.

headline: Nakunaru is literally “to become not”: the -ku form of 無い (nai, “not, missing”) plus なる (naru).

sources.quote: The adverbial -く (-ku) form of adjective 無い (nai, “not, missing, not present”) + verb なる (naru, “to become”): literally, "to become not, to become nonexistent".
The 亡 spelling of the na- root of nai and naku naru is reserved for the meaning of "dead, gone".
Cognate with 無(な)くなる (naku naru).

headline: Fun'iki appeared in a physics book of 1827, translating Dutch lucht (“air”), before it came to mean “atmosphere”.

sources.quote: Appeared in the book on physics 気海観瀾 (Kikai Kanran) of 1827. Until the end of the Edo period, the term was used as a translation of Dutch lucht (“air”). In the early Meiji period, it became common as a translation of English atmosphere, and in the late Meiji period, it changed to an abstract meaning as it is today.

headline: Shi, “death”, appears to be a conflation of Middle Chinese 死 with an Old Japanese root that sounded alike.

sources.quote: /si/ → /ɕi/

Appears to be a conflation of Middle Chinese 死 (MC sijX), with an Old Japanese root that happened to have a similar pronunciation to the Middle Chinese and was probably cognate with 去る (saru, “to go, to go away”). Compare modern Mandarin 死 (sǐ).
In kanji compounds, this would be considered as on'yomi; but on its own, this could be considered as either on'yomi or kun'yomi.

headline: Shōgakukin is 奨学 (shōgaku) plus 金 (-kin).

sources.quote: 奨学(しょうがく) (shōgaku) + 金(きん) (-kin)

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Ultimate derivation unknown.

headline: Ka, “passable”, is from Middle Chinese 可.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 可 (MC khaX).

headline: Fujin, “madam”, is described as simply from Classical Chinese.

sources.quote: From Classical Chinese.

headline: Gan, “cancer”, is from Middle Chinese 癌.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 癌.

headline: Iremono is the verb 入れる (ireru) plus 物 (-mono).

sources.quote: 入(い)れる (ireru) + 物(もの) (-mono)

meaning: to be popular, to come into fashion
headline: Hayaru is related to 早い (hayai, “early, fast”), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *paya.

sources.quote: Related to 早(はや)い (hayai, “early, fast”) and 逸(はや)る (hayaru, “to be impatient”), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *paya.

headline: Semaru, “to draw near”, is cognate with 攻める (semeru) and 狭い (semai).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Cognate with 攻(せ)める (semeru), 責(せ)める (semeru), 狭(せば)める (sebameru), 狭(せば)まる (sebamaru), and 狭(せま)い (semai).

headline: Bangumi is 番 (ban, “turn”) plus 組み (kumi), with the k voiced to g by rendaku.

sources.quote: Compound of 番(ばん) (ban, “turn”) + 組(ぐ)み (-gumi, “set (of items)”). The kumi changes to gumi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Aware originally meant “deeply touching or moving”, with no negative connotation.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Originally meant "deeply touching or moving", without a negative connotation.

headline: Uraguchi is 裏 (ura, “back”) plus 口 (kuchi, “opening, door”), with kuchi voiced to guchi.

sources.quote: 裏(うら) (ura, “back”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “opening, door”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Aku, “evil”, is from Middle Chinese 惡.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 惡 (MC 'ak).

headline: Masukomi is short for masu komyunikēshon, “mass communication”.

sources.quote: Short for マスコミュニケーション (masu komyunikēshon).
